title: AnyBlock JSON property dictionary
description: One properties.json at the root of a bundle names every property the bundle's objects use — the dictionary (§2f). It is a sibling of index.json, not a section inside it: an index says where things are, a dictionary says what they mean. A bundle carries no property document at all (§15 #23): this file is where every property something references is stated — replacing the ~9,500 documents per account (kind "property") that restated the bundled table field for field (98% of installed copies are identical to it), and the rest besides — and it is what lets a third-party reader interpret a backup WITHOUT shipping the bundled table: every entry carries its format, so a date is a date and an option name is an option name even to a reader that has never seen Anytype.

$schema.description: Which of the format's three grammars this document follows — an object document, a bundle index, or a property dictionary. OPTIONAL and DECORATIVE for validity: `formatVersion` alone gates the format, so a stale or invented URL here never makes a document invalid. What it does do is DISPATCH: a reader handed a file with no filename to go by uses this to pick the grammar, matching on the trailing `object|index|properties.schema.json` and ignoring the version segment. Without it a reader falls back to the document's shape, which can only tell the grammars apart when the document happens to carry a member unique to one. Every document this format writes carries it, and a hand-written one is easier for a reader to place if it does too.

properties.description: One propertyDefinition per property the bundle's objects actually REFERENCE — used-only, not everything the space holds: a space installs a median 125 bundled properties and uses 57, and the 68 nothing touches buy a reader nothing (the restore reinstalls the bundled table anyway). A property nothing references is not exported at all — no document (a bundle carries none, §15 #23), no entry: nothing names the key, so there is no value to explain and no format to look up. This is the dictionary's ONE list (§15 #24): a bundled property the bundle carries is an entry here like any other, and every entry states the COMPLETE definition — name, format, description, object types, include-time on a date, max count on a format that can hold more than one value, readonly, default value, options, the entry's own flags — whatever the property has and its format leaves room for, whether the key is bundled or space-minted, whether the space's copy matched the shipped table or not (§15 #25). There is no reduced entry that leaves a reader to fill the rest from its own table, and no reader needs the table to interpret the file. A reader tells a bundled key from a space-minted one by looking the stored key up in its own shipped table, the lookup every §3 slot runs, never by a flag on the entry; `bundled_diverged` is not that flag — it says a bundled key's copy had DIVERGED from the table at export time, and its absence says nothing about bundled-ness. Keys are CANONICAL SPELLINGS: the display name from the shipped table for a bundled key, the stored key verbatim for a space-minted one — a pure function of the key, because this file carries no legend. The reader flow is object → spelling → (1) the document's property_internal_keys legend, (2) a verbatim match against a dictionary key, (3) the shipped name table over the dictionary's own keys, with the forgiving fold behind it for near-misses and pre-v0.48 derived-slug spellings. Step 3 carries most value slots, because §3 writes a legend line only for a spelling the bundled table does not bind. Look up, never transform: the name and the key say different words (`Creation date` / `createdDate`). No folder convention, no scanning (§2f).

dictionaryEntry.description:
One dictionary entry: a propertyDefinition (§2e), referenced rather than restated. Its `property` is the entry's spelling: the display name for a bundled property (`Due date`), the stored key verbatim for a space-minted one — a bson id like `6a32d4856761631534b22f85`, from which nothing must ever be derived. Its `internal_key` is the stored key itself, written by export for fidelity and never required from an author. This is the third of the shape's three homes, beside a type document's property-definition entry and a property document's property_settings — and the only one a bundle this format's composer writes (§15 #23), which is why its owned members — `hidden`, `bundled_diverged`, `api_key` and, shared with a type's declaration, `uninstalled` — carry what a property document used to: the three flags only the export could know, and the stored api key no restore re-derives. Three of the four are the entry's alone; `uninstalled` is stated by a type's `property_definitions` entry as well, because that entry is a complete standalone definition too and a definition that presents a removed property as live is not complete. The layer narrows `object_types` to a real array (only a property document's STORED value can hold a null; a dictionary describes, it does not mirror a store slot) and requires `format`, because self-sufficiency is the constraint that shapes the dictionary: an entry without a format is readable only by a reader shipping the same bundled vocabulary, which is exactly the dependence the dictionary exists to end. An entry must identify the property it declares: state a `property` (the spelling), or an `internal_key` (the stored id), or a `name` the spelling is derived from. A NAME ALONE IS ENOUGH — `{"name": "Cooking Time", "format": "number"}` declares a property spelled `Cooking Time`. Prefer `property` or `name` when authoring: `internal_key` is an id the app mints, an author has no space to draw one from, and inventing one is never right — when a custom property states none, the import wiring mints a fresh internal key exactly as the app does when a user creates one. A derived spelling runs through the same resolution as a written one, so a property named "Due Date" folds onto the bundled `dueDate` instead of minting a lookalike beside it.

CARDINALITY IS NOT A MEMBER of this entry, and does not need to be. On a format that holds a LIST — objects, files, select, multi_select, properties — a value may be written as the bare value or as a one-element array holding it, and the two are THE SAME VALUE: both store one list and both re-export as the array, so the shape a document happens to use carries nothing a reader can get wrong. The equivalence runs in that direction only: on a single-valued format an array is not unwrapped, so `["hi"]` on a text property is a list of strings and stays one. `max_count` is the only thing the entry says about how many values fit, and it is written only where the format leaves room for more than one.

allOf.description: Which shape this entry has. An entry is a propertyDefinition (§2e) — the shared shape, referenced across files by its published URL — UNLESS its format is the sentinel `unknown`, which says no definition could be found for the key at all. The two are not narrowings of one another: a definition states what a property holds, and `unknown` states that nothing states it, so the `unknown` branch REPLACES the shared shape instead of layering over it.

name.description: When name supplies the property identity, readers NFC-normalize it before applying the 128-character writable-key bound. Standard JSON Schema cannot count characters after normalization, so this schema enforces the expressible non-empty/control-free part and semantic readers enforce the normalized maximum.

object_types.description: objects/files only: the types the property may point at, in priority order, each written as the type's derived id `type-<internal_key>` (§9); a display name or the legacy `ot-<key>` is accepted on input.

value_names.description:
The complete set of names a value of this property can be — the entry's answer to the one question a bundle could not otherwise answer about its own bytes. Written for the properties whose stored value is a NUMBER whose meaning is an app enum and whose exported value is that enum's NAME (§3): `layout`, `resolvedLayout`, `layoutAlign`, `origin`, `importType`, `imageKind`, `participantPermissions`, `participantStatus`, and `recommendedLayout`, which a type document carries as `type_settings.layout`. Written only where the entry itself states `"format": "number"` — the encoder's table is keyed on the stored key, while an entry states the format the SPACE holds, and a copy that has diverged from the bundled table could otherwise publish a number's names beside a format that holds no numbers. Sorted, complete, and DERIVED from the encoder's own table, so the published list cannot say something export has stopped writing.

It exists because `format` alone is a lie of omission on exactly these keys. The entry says `"format": "number"` — the stored format, correctly — while every value in the bundle is a string: across a 79-bundle corpus all 62,325 values in the six object-carried slots of the seven keys named first are strings and not one is a number. (The participant pair was named after that corpus was taken, and its 5,038 slots are bare integers in every bundle of it — the last of these gaps to close, and the largest.) A reader holding only the bundle could not learn the members from anywhere: object.schema.json publishes enum vocabularies for the slots that constrain them, not for a property value, and `$defs/propertyMap` accepts any value at all. So the reader guesses, and the entry's own `description` tells it to guess WRONG: `layout`'s reads "Anytype layout ID(from pb enum)", which is the store's own text describing the STORED number, and a reader that believes it writes `"Layout": 1`; `participantPermissions`' reads "Possible values: models.ParticipantPermissions", a pointer to a Go symbol in a repository the bundle does not ship. That write is refused now, naming the value 1 stands for — but the refusal is the second line of defence and this member is the first. Read `format` with `value_names`, never `description`: a description is free text a user may have edited, while this list is the encoder's.

READ-facing, and not an authoring surface. Export writes it; an author never does, and one written by hand is answered with a warning rather than obeyed — the format enforces no vocabulary an entry invents, and it does not take the entry's word for one it owns. All nine of these keys are hidden, readonly or both in the shipped table, so the member states what a value MEANS, never what a caller may choose. These keys are single-valued, so a value is one of these names written bare: an array is not unwrapped on a single-valued format, and `["profile"]` is a different stored value from `"profile"` — a list of strings sitting on a number-format key, which nothing reads as a layout.

Absence says only that THIS entry publishes no vocabulary. Usually that is because the property has none — most properties do not — and on an entry whose `format` is not `number` it is because the names of a number are not that entry's to publish, which a diverged copy of a named key can reach. It never means the writer omitted a list it had.

uninstalled.description: The user REMOVED this property from the space, and the bundle carries it for backup fidelity rather than as a document (§2f, §15 #22). Export writes `true` only; absent is the same statement as `false`, and an author never writes it — there is nothing to uninstall in a bundle that has not been installed. A reader MAY recreate the property with its removal mark set, or skip it: a removed property appears in no listing either way, so both restores look the same, and the entry still says what a value stored under the key means. What a reader MUST NOT do is install it as a live property. The flag is the whole statement of the removal (§15 #24): the dictionary keeps no list of installed keys for it to contradict. A member of the dictionary entry only: on a type's property_definitions entry or a property document's property_settings it would describe nothing, and both homes refuse it, as this one refuses `section`.

api_key.description: The property's public API key (stored `apiObjectKey`) — the spelling callers address it by on the API surface. NOT a slug of the name: an api key does not follow a rename and nothing rewrites it, so `Location` keeps `restaurant_location`. It travels because no restore mints one — the rule that derives an api key lives on the app's create path and an import does not take it — and since §15 #23 a bundle writes no property document, so this entry is the only place the stored value can travel. Export writes it where the store holds one; an author never writes one. A member of the dictionary entry only: a type's declaration says how THAT type uses a property, and the property's public address is not one of the things it says.

hidden.description: The store HIDES this property from every listing (its stored `isHidden`), and a bundle carries no property document to say so (§2f, §15 #23), so the entry does. Export writes `true` only; absent is the same statement as `false`, and an author never writes it — a property is declared to be used, and hiding one is a store fact the export records, like `internal_key`. A reader that recreates the property sets the mark; a reader that only interprets values ignores it. Distinct from a type declaration's `section`, which says where a property sits on ONE type: `hidden` says whether the property is shown at all. A member of the dictionary entry only, on the same footing as `uninstalled`: the shape's other two homes refuse it.

bundled_diverged.description: The space's copy of a BUNDLED property — a key the shipped table names — had DIVERGED from that table when the bundle was written (§2f, §15 #25): a rename, a changed description or hidden bit, any definition member. The entry states the user's version, complete, like every entry; this member says that version is the user's and not the table's, so a reader restoring the key takes the entry over its own table. It is written because it is NOT derivable: a reader could diff the entry against its table today, but the shipped table moves between app versions — once Anytype renames a bundled property, a later reader cannot tell whether the user renamed it or the table did. The verdict is knowable only at export time, and this records it. Export writes `true` only, and only for a key in the writer's shipped table whose copy the identity check refused; absent means EITHER "not a bundled property" OR "bundled and not diverged", and the reader separates those with the table lookup it already runs for every key (§15 #24) — this is not a `bundled` flag. Reader behaviour: key in the reader's table and no flag → install the fresh bundled property, accepting any newer name the table has; key in the table with `bundled_diverged: true` → the user's version wins, create or update from the entry; key not in the reader's table → create from the entry, flag or no flag. An author never writes it — there is no space whose copy could have diverged. A member of the dictionary entry only, on the same footing as `uninstalled` and `hidden`: the shape's other two homes refuse it.

undefinedPropertyEntry.description:
An entry for a property key the bundle's documents REFERENCE and nothing could define — almost always a relation the user deleted, whose definition went with it. In one audited 3,286-document space that is 628 values across 313 documents naming 153 such keys, and their values are uninterpretable on sight: `"66602dc5e5672d06c0e19245": 1717538400` could be a date, a count or an id, and nothing in that bundle can tell — it has no entry, no type declaration, no format cached on a dataview column, and one legend line spelling the key as itself. A key a type document DECLARES is not one of these: a declaration states a name and a format, so the writer takes them and this entry is not what it writes (that is 4 keys over a 79-bundle corpus, 2 of them in this space, and it is why the counts here are lower than an earlier measurement of the same export). Without an entry the key resolves to NOTHING in this file, and a reader cannot tell "the writer had nothing to say" from "I failed to look". This is that distinction, made once: every referenced key resolves to something, and for some of them the something is that there is no answer. How much was lost, and to how many keys, is stated in index.json rather than counted here.

`unknown` is NOT a property format. It is absent from `$defs/propertyFormat`, the one list every format slot in the format references, so a type's `property_definitions` entry, a dataview property and a property document's own `property_settings` all refuse it — a declaration says how a property is USED, and an absent definition is not a use. It is absent from the authoring subset for the same reason from the other side: an author declaring a property always knows what it holds, and this member exists for what an EXPORT found it could not describe.

An entry that states it states NOTHING ELSE — no name, no description, no options, no target types, no flags, no `value_names`. There is nothing else to state, and that is the whole content of the claim: an entry carrying a format's worth of detail beside `unknown` would be describing a definition it has just said it does not have. Identity is all that remains, and identity is the point — the key, so the reference resolves. A `name` was admitted here once, for "a legend line, a type's declaration", and no writer ever wrote one: a legend line binds a spelling to a stored key and carries no name, and a type's declaration states a format beside its name, which makes it a definition and this shape not what the writer reaches for.

A reader MUST NOT create a property from one of these. There is nothing to create: no format, no name the store ever held. What it may do is read the values under the key as the raw JSON they are, and say so — which is exactly what the writer knew.

property.description: The entry's spelling, as on any entry (§2f): for a key nothing defines this is the stored key verbatim, because a key the bundled table does not name has no other pure spelling and nothing may ever be derived from a bson id.

internal_key.description: The stored key itself — the thing the documents' values are keyed by, and the reason the entry exists.

format.description: The sentinel: no definition of this property could be found. Not a format — see this shape's description.
